title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Quickly generate 30 random walks 100 steps . Usage: Parameters: None Returns: Tibble 3,000 rows (30 walks × 100 steps) Columns: - walk_number: Factor identifying walk - step_number: Integer step counter (1-100) - y: Random walk values - cum_sum, cum_prod, cum_min, cum_max, cum_mean: Cumulative functions can added returned Examples:
code: rw30() # Generate and view rw30() |> head(10) #> # A tibble: 10 × 3 #>    walk_number step_number     y #>    <fct>             <int> <dbl> #>  1 1                     1  0    #>  2 1                     2 -1.40 #>  3 1                     3 -1.14 #>  4 1                     4 -3.58 #>  5 1                     5 -3.59 #>  6 1                     6 -2.97 #>  7 1                     7 -1.82 #>  8 1                     8 -3.64 #>  9 1                     9 -3.89 #> 10 1                    10 -4.13 # Visualize rw30() |> visualize_walks() # Analyze rw30() |> summarize_walks(.value = y) |> head() #> Warning: There was 1 warning in `dplyr::summarize()`. #> ℹ In argument: `geometric_mean = exp(mean(log(y)))`. #> Caused by warning in `log()`: #> ! NaNs produced #> # A tibble: 1 × 16 #>   fns   fns_name dimensions mean_val median range quantile_lo quantile_hi #>   <chr> <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 rw30  Rw30              1    0.467  0.355  47.2       -12.7        12.6 #> # ℹ 8 more variables: variance <dbl>, sd <dbl>, min_val <dbl>, max_val <dbl>, #> #   harmonic_mean <dbl>, geometric_mean <dbl>, skewness <dbl>, kurtosis <dbl>

title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Create comprehensive visualizations random walks. Parameters: - .data: Random walk data (tibble) - .alpha: Line transparency, 0-1 (default: 0.7) - .interactive: Boolean, create interactive plot (default: FALSE) - .pluck: Select specific columns plot (default: FALSE shows ) - Use exact plotted column names "y", "cum_sum_y", "cum_sum_x", "cum_sum_z" - Short cumulative aliases "cum_sum" work match exactly one plotted column - Can vector: c("y", "cum_sum_y") Returns: - Static mode: ggplot2/patchwork object - Interactive mode: ggiraph object Examples:
code: # Basic visualization rw30() |> visualize_walks() # Adjust transparency rw30() |> visualize_walks(.alpha = 0.3) # Interactive (not run in vignette) rw30() |> visualize_walks(.interactive = TRUE)  # Select specific panels random_normal_walk() |> visualize_walks(.pluck = "cum_sum_y") random_normal_walk() |> visualize_walks(.pluck = c("y", "cum_sum_y", "cum_mean_y"))

title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Extract walks extreme values. Parameters: - .data: Random walk data (tibble) - .value: Column name subset (default: “y”) - .type: Type subset (“max”, “min”, “”) Returns: Tibble containing selected walk Examples:
code: # Walk with maximum value walks |> subset_walks(.type = "max", .value = "y")  # Walk with minimum value walks |> subset_walks(.type = "min", .value = "y")

title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Calculate confidence interval vector. Parameters: - .x: Numeric vector - .interval: Confidence level (default: 0.95 95% CI) Returns: Tibble columns: - lower: Lower confidence bound - upper: Upper confidence bound Example:
code: x <- rnorm(1000, mean = 10, sd = 2) confidence_interval(x)  # 99% CI confidence_interval(x, .interval = 0.99)

title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Calculate running quantile position. Parameters: - .x: Numeric vector - .probs: Probability value (0-1) - .window: Window size (positive integer; number points include running quantile calculation) Returns: Numeric vector length Example:
code: x <- rnorm(100) running_quantile(x, .probs = 0.5, .window = 5)  # Running median

title: RandomWalker API Reference
text: Calculate Euclidean distance origin multi-dimensional walks. Parameters: - .data: Multi-dimensional random walk data (tibble) Returns: Original data added distance column Example:
code: walk_2d <- random_normal_walk(.dimensions = 2) walk_2d |> euclidean_distance(.x = x, .y = y)

title: Automatic Random Walks
text: rw30() function: 1. Generates 30 random walks 2. 100 steps 3. Using normal distribution (mean = 0, sd = 1) 4. Starting 0 5. Returns tidy tibble ’s equivalent :
code: random_normal_walk(   .num_walks = 30,   .n = 100,   .mu = 0,   .sd = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .dimensions = 1 )

title: Automatic Random Walks
text: Columns: - walk_number: Factor (1-30) identifying walk - step_number: Integer (1-100) step - y: random walk values Note: Cumulative columns cum_sum, cum_prod, cum_min, cum_max, cum_mean included default. can add using rand_walk_helper() tidyverse operations needed. ## Understanding Output

code: # Test if variance grows linearly with steps walks <- rw30()  variance_by_step <- walks |>   group_by(step_number) |>   reframe(     variance = var(y),     theoretical = step_number  # For N(0,1), var = n   )  ggplot(variance_by_step, aes(x = step_number)) +   geom_line(aes(y = variance, color = "Observed"), linewidth = 1) +   geom_line(aes(y = theoretical, color = "Theoretical"), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "blue", "Theoretical" = "red")) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Variance Growth in Random Walk",     subtitle = "Observed vs Theoretical (Var = n)",     x = "Step Number",     y = "Variance",     color = ""   )

title: Automatic Random Walks
code: # Generate walks walks <- rw30()  # Show that mean displacement is zero walks |>   group_by(step_number) |>   summarize(mean_position = mean(y)) |>   ggplot(aes(x = step_number, y = mean_position)) +   geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Mean Position Over Time",     subtitle = "Averages to zero (red line)",     x = "Step",     y = "Mean Position"   ) # Show that standard deviation grows as sqrt(n) walks |>   group_by(step_number) |>   reframe(     sd_position = sd(y),     theoretical = sqrt(step_number)   ) |>   ungroup() |>   ggplot(aes(x = step_number)) +   geom_line(aes(y = sd_position, color = "Observed"), linewidth = 1) +   geom_line(aes(y = theoretical, color = "Theoretical"), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "blue", "Theoretical" = "red")) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Standard Deviation Growth",     subtitle = "Should follow sqrt(n) (red dashed line)",     x = "Step",     y = "Standard Deviation",     color = ""   )

title: Automatic Random Walks
code: # Find when walks first cross a threshold walks <- rw30()  first_crossing <- walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   filter(y >= 5) |>   slice_min(step_number, n = 1) |>   select(walk_number, first_crossing_time = step_number)  # Some walks may never cross n_crossed <- nrow(first_crossing) cat(sprintf("%d out of 30 walks crossed 5\n", n_crossed)) #> 12 out of 30 walks crossed 5  # Distribution of first crossing times if (n_crossed > 0) {   ggplot(first_crossing, aes(x = first_crossing_time)) +     geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +     theme_minimal() +     labs(       title = "First Passage Time Distribution",       subtitle = "Time to first cross level 5",       x = "Step Number",       y = "Count"     ) }

code: # Find maximum distance from origin walks <- rw30()  max_excursion <- walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   summarize(     max_positive = max(y),     max_negative = min(y),     max_excursion = max(abs(y))   )  # Visualize max_excursion |>   ggplot(aes(x = max_excursion)) +   geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Distribution of Maximum Excursions",     subtitle = "Maximum absolute distance from origin",     x = "Maximum Excursion",     y = "Count"   )

title: Basic Concepts
text: Imagine flipping coin: - Heads: Move one step forward (+1) - Tails: Move one step backward (-1) - Start: Position 0 10 flips, might position +2, -4, anywhere else. random walk!

title: Basic Concepts
text: 1D symmetric walk: - Probability eventual return = 1 (certain return) - Expected return time = ∞ (infinite expected time!) 2D symmetric walk: - Probability eventual return = 1 3D symmetric walk: - Probability eventual return ≈ 0.34 (certain!)

title: Basic Concepts
text: Random walks exhibit scaling invariance: - zoom factor k - Time scales k² - Position scales k

title: Basic Concepts
text: Position n steps: Δᵢ independent random steps. standard normal walk: - Δᵢ ~ N(0, 1) - X(n) ~ N(0, n) - E[X(n)] = 0 - Var[X(n)] = n
code: X(n) = X(0) + Σ(i=1 to n) Δᵢ

title: Basic Concepts
text: Continuous-time stochastic process: : - μ = drift coefficient - σ = volatility coefficient - W(t) = standard Wiener process Properties: - W(0) = 0 - W(t) ~ N(0, t) - W(t) - W(s) ~ N(0, t-s) t > s - Independent increments
code: dX(t) = μ dt + σ dW(t)

title: Basic Concepts
text: stock prices: Solution: Properties: - Always positive - Log-normal distribution - Used Black-Scholes model
code: dS(t) = μ S(t) dt + σ S(t) dW(t) S(t) = S(0) exp((μ - σ²/2)t + σW(t))

code: # What rw30() does internally:  # 1. Generate random steps steps <- rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # 2. Compute cumulative sum positions <- cumsum(c(0, steps[-100]))  # 3. Add to tibble walk_data <- dplyr::tibble(   step_number = 1:100,   y = steps,   cum_sum = positions )  # 4. Add more cumulative functions walk_data <- walk_data |>   mutate(     cum_prod = cumprod(1 + y),     cum_min = cummin(y),     cum_max = cummax(y),     cum_mean = cumsum(y) / step_number   )  walk_data |> head(10) #> # A tibble: 10 × 7 #>    step_number      y cum_sum cum_prod cum_min cum_max cum_mean #>          <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> #>  1           1 -1.18   0       -0.176    -1.18  -1.18  -1.18    #>  2           2  0.607 -1.18    -0.282    -1.18   0.607 -0.284   #>  3           3  0.552 -0.569   -0.438    -1.18   0.607 -0.00553 #>  4           4  0.455 -0.0166  -0.637    -1.18   0.607  0.110   #>  5           5  0.181  0.438   -0.752    -1.18   0.607  0.124   #>  6           6 -1.25   0.619    0.187    -1.25   0.607 -0.105   #>  7           7  1.67  -0.630    0.499    -1.25   1.67   0.148   #>  8           8 -0.761  1.04     0.120    -1.25   1.67   0.0346  #>  9           9  1.14   0.277    0.256    -1.25   1.67   0.157   #> 10          10 -0.644  1.42     0.0910   -1.25   1.67   0.0772

title: Basic Concepts
text: 1D Walk: - Single value per step: y - Position: cum_sum 2D Walk: - Two values per step: x, y - Position: (cum_sum_x, cum_sum_y) - Distance: sqrt(cum_sum_x² + cum_sum_y²) 3D Walk: - Three values per step: x, y, z - Position: (cum_sum_x, cum_sum_y, cum_sum_z) - Distance: sqrt(cum_sum_x² + cum_sum_y² + cum_sum_z²)

title: Basic Concepts
text: Random walks path-dependent - ending doesn’t tell route:
code: # Generate walks ending at similar positions set.seed(123) walks <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 100)  # Find walks ending near 10 similar_end <- walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   filter(step_number == 80, abs(cum_sum_y - 1) < 0.5)  # Plot their paths - very different! walks |>   filter(walk_number %in% similar_end$walk_number) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "cum_sum_y", .alpha = 0.5)

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: commonly used random walk, based normal (Gaussian) distribution. Function Signature: Distribution Parameters: - .mu - Mean distribution (default: 0) - .sd - Standard deviation (default: 1) Use Cases: - General-purpose random walks - Modeling measurement errors - Simulating natural phenomena normal noise Example:
code: random_normal_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .mu = 0,   .sd = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Basic normal walk random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 10, .n = 100) |>   visualize_walks() # With custom mean and SD random_normal_walk(   .num_walks = 5,   .n = 200,   .mu = 0.01,    # Slight upward drift   .sd = 0.5,     # Lower volatility   .initial_value = 100 ) |> visualize_walks() # 2D spatial walk random_normal_walk(   .num_walks = 3,   .n = 500,   .dimensions = 2 ) |> visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk deterministic drift component. Function Signature: Key Difference random_normal_walk(): - .drift - Drift term added step (default: 0.1) - Adds explicit drift term: drift + random_step - pronounced trending behavior - Better modeling processes clear directional movement Example:
code: random_normal_drift_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .mu = 0,   .sd = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Compare walks with and without drift p1 <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 5, .mu = 0.1) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") +   labs(title = "Normal Walk")  p2 <- random_normal_drift_walk(.num_walks = 5, .mu = 0.1) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") +   labs(title = "Normal Walk with Drift")  p1 / p2

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Standard Brownian motion (Wiener process) - foundation stochastic calculus. Function Signature: Parameters: - .num_walks - Number walks generate (default: 25) - .n - Number steps per walk (default: 100) - .delta_time - Time increment per step (default: 1) - .initial_value - Starting value walk (default: 0) - .dimensions - Number dimensions (default: 1) Mathematical Form: Use Cases: - Financial mathematics (Black-Scholes model) - Physics (particle diffusion) - Signal processing (noise modeling) Example:
code: brownian_motion(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .delta_time = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Standard Brownian motion brownian_motion(.num_walks = 10) |>   visualize_walks() # With drift and volatility brownian_motion(   .num_walks = 50,   .n = 252,   .delta_time = 0.05,   .initial_value = 100 ) |> visualize_walks(.alpha = 0.3)

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Geometric Brownian motion - standard model stock prices. Function Signature: Parameters: - .mu - Expected return (drift) - .sigma - Volatility Mathematical Form: Key Properties: - Always positive (can’t go zero) - Log-normal distribution prices - Percentage changes normally distributed Use Cases: - Stock price modeling - Option pricing - Asset allocation simulations - Monte Carlo risk analysis Example:
code: geometric_brownian_motion(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .mu = 0,   .sigma = 0.1,   .initial_value = 100,   .delta_time = 0.003,   .dimensions = 1 ) dS(t) = μ S(t) dt + σ S(t) dW(t) S(t) = S(0) exp((μ - σ²/2)t + σW(t)) # Model stock prices stock_sim <- geometric_brownian_motion(   .num_walks = 1000,   .n = 252,        # Trading days in a year   .mu = 0.08,      # 8% expected return   .sigma = 0.25,   # 25% volatility   .initial_value = 100 )  # Visualize scenarios stock_sim |> visualize_walks(.alpha = 0.1) # Analyze outcomes stock_sim |>   summarize_walks(.value = cum_prod_y, .group_var = walk_number) |>   summarize(     median_price = median(max_val),     prob_profit = mean(max_val > 100),     prob_loss_50 = mean(min_val < 50)   )

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based beta distribution (bounded 0 1). Function Signature: Parameters: - .shape1 - First shape parameter (α) - .shape2 - Second shape parameter (β) - .ncp - Non-centrality parameter (default: 0) Properties: - Steps bounded: 0 ≤ step ≤ 1 - Flexible shapes (uniform, U-shaped, bell-shaped) - Mean = α / (α + β) - Variance = (α β) / ((α + β)² (α + β + 1)) Shape Guide: - shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1: Uniform (0,1) - shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2: Symmetric, bell-shaped - shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5: Right-skewed - shape1 = 5, shape2 = 2: Left-skewed Use Cases: - Modeling proportions percentages - Bounded processes (e.g., utilization rates) - Success rates time Example:
code: random_beta_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .shape1 = 2,   .shape2 = 2,   .ncp = 0,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Symmetric beta walk random_beta_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .shape1 = 2,   .shape2 = 2 ) |> visualize_walks() # Right-skewed (toward 0) random_beta_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .shape1 = 2,   .shape2 = 5 ) |> visualize_walks() # Compare different shapes p1 <- random_beta_walk(.shape1 = 1, .shape2 = 1) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") p2 <- random_beta_walk(.shape1 = 2, .shape2 = 5) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") p1 / p2

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk heavy tails - extreme values much common normal distribution. Function Signature: Parameters: - .location - Location parameter (median) - .scale - Scale parameter (spread) Properties: - defined mean variance! - Heavy tails (high probability extreme values) - Symmetric around location - Much volatile normal distribution Use Cases: - Modeling extreme events - Financial crises simulation - Physics (resonance phenomena) - Robust statistics demonstrations Example:
code: random_cauchy_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .location = 0,   .scale = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Standard Cauchy walk random_cauchy_walk(.num_walks = 10) |>   visualize_walks() # Compare with normal walk p1 <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 5, .sd = 1) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") +   labs(title = "Normal Walk")  p2 <- random_cauchy_walk(.num_walks = 5, .scale = 1) |>   visualize_walks(.pluck = "y") +   labs(title = "Cauchy Walk (Heavy Tails)")  p1 / p2

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based chi-squared distribution (always positive). Function Signature: Parameters: - .df - Degrees freedom - .ncp - Non-centrality parameter (default: 0) Properties: - Steps always positive - Right-skewed (especially low df) - Mean = df - Variance = 2df Use Cases: - Goodness--fit tests - Variance estimation - Quality control - Reliability engineering Example:
code: random_chisquared_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .df = 5,   .ncp = 0,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Low df (very skewed) random_chisquared_walk(.num_walks = 10, .df = 1) |>   visualize_walks() # Higher df (more symmetric) random_chisquared_walk(.num_walks = 10, .df = 10) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk exponentially distributed steps (memoryless property). Function Signature: Parameters: - .rate - Rate parameter (λ) Properties: - Steps always positive - Memoryless property - Mean = 1/rate - Variance = 1/rate² Use Cases: - Time events (queuing theory) - Lifetime modeling - Radioactive decay - Poisson process intervals Example:
code: random_exponential_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .rate = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Standard exponential random_exponential_walk(.num_walks = 10) |>   visualize_walks() # Fast rate (smaller steps) random_exponential_walk(.num_walks = 10, .rate = 5) |>   visualize_walks() # Slow rate (larger steps) random_exponential_walk(.num_walks = 10, .rate = 0.5) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based F-distribution (ratio chi-squared variables). Function Signature: Parameters: - .df1 - Numerator degrees freedom - .df2 - Denominator degrees freedom - .ncp - Non-centrality parameter Use Cases: - ANOVA - Variance ratio tests - Model comparison Example:
code: random_f_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .df1 = 5,   .df2 = 5,   .ncp = NULL,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_f_walk(.num_walks = 10, .df1 = 5, .df2 = 10) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Flexible distribution positive values. Function Signature: Parameters: - .shape - Shape parameter (k) - .rate - Rate parameter (β) - .scale - Scale parameter (1/rate) Properties: - Steps always positive - Flexible shapes - Mean = shape/rate - Variance = shape/rate² Use Cases: - Waiting times - Rainfall modeling - Insurance claims - Reliability analysis Example:
code: random_gamma_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .shape = 1,   .scale = 1,   .rate = NULL,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Different shape parameters random_gamma_walk(.num_walks = 10, .shape = 1, .rate = 1) |>   visualize_walks() random_gamma_walk(.num_walks = 10, .shape = 5, .rate = 1) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk log steps normally distributed. Function Signature: Parameters: - .meanlog - Mean log - .sdlog - Standard deviation log Properties: - Steps always positive - Right-skewed - Multiplicative processes Use Cases: - Income distributions - File sizes - Particle sizes - Stock prices (alternative GBM) Example:
code: random_lognormal_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .meanlog = 0,   .sdlog = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_lognormal_walk(.num_walks = 10) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk logistic distribution (heavier tails normal). Function Signature: Use Cases: - Growth models - Binary classification - Neural networks Example:
code: random_logistic_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .location = 0,   .scale = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_logistic_walk(.num_walks = 10) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk t-distribution (adjustable tail heaviness). Function Signature: Parameters: - .df - Degrees freedom (controls tail heaviness) - .ncp - Non-centrality parameter Properties: - Heavier tails normal (low df) - Approaches normal df → ∞ - Mean = 0 (df > 1) - Variance = df/(df-2) (df > 2) Use Cases: - Robust statistics - Small sample inference - Financial returns modeling Example:
code: random_t_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .df = 5,   .initial_value = 0,   .ncp = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Heavy tails (df = 3) random_t_walk(.num_walks = 10, .df = 3) |>   visualize_walks() # Nearly normal (df = 30) random_t_walk(.num_walks = 10, .df = 30) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk uniformly distributed steps. Function Signature: Parameters: - .min - Minimum value - .max - Maximum value Properties: - values equally likely - Mean = (min + max) / 2 - Variance = (max - min)² / 12 Use Cases: - Modeling equal probabilities - Random sampling - Monte Carlo simulations Example:
code: random_uniform_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .min = 0,   .max = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Symmetric around 0 random_uniform_walk(.num_walks = 10, .min = -1, .max = 1) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Continuous Distribution Generators
text: Random walk Weibull distribution (flexible lifetime model). Function Signature: Parameters: - .shape - Shape parameter (k) - .scale - Scale parameter (λ) Properties: - Steps always positive - shape < 1: Decreasing failure rate - shape = 1: Constant failure rate (exponential) - shape > 1: Increasing failure rate Use Cases: - Reliability engineering - Survival analysis - Wind speed modeling - Materials science Example:
code: random_weibull_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .shape = 1,   .scale = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Different shape parameters random_weibull_walk(.num_walks = 10, .shape = 0.5) |>   visualize_walks() random_weibull_walk(.num_walks = 10, .shape = 2) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: fundamental discrete random walk binary outcomes (). Function Signature: Parameters: - .upper_bound - Maximum step size (default: 1) - .lower_bound - Minimum step size (default: -1) - .upper_probability - Probability moving (default: 0.5) Properties: - Simple binary outcomes - step either .upper_bound .lower_bound - Unbiased .upper_probability = 0.5 - Can create biased walks adjusting probability Use Cases: - Gambler’s ruin problem - Simple gain/loss scenarios - Teaching probability concepts - Binary decision modeling Example:
code: discrete_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .upper_bound = 1,   .lower_bound = -1,   .upper_probability = 0.5,   .initial_value = 100,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Unbiased walk (50/50) discrete_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .n = 100,   .upper_probability = 0.5 ) |> visualize_walks() # Biased upward (60% up, 40% down) discrete_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .n = 100,   .upper_probability = 0.6 ) |> visualize_walks() # Gambler's ruin simulation gambler <- discrete_walk(   .num_walks = 100,   .n = 1000,   .upper_bound = 1,   .lower_bound = -1,   .upper_probability = 0.48,  # House edge   .initial_value = 100 )  gambler |>   summarize_walks(.value = cum_sum_y, .group_var = walk_number) |>   summarize(     prob_ruin = mean(min_val <= 0),     avg_final = mean(max_val)   ) #> Warning: There were 5 warnings in `dplyr::summarize()`. #> The first warning was: #> ℹ In argument: `geometric_mean = exp(mean(log(cum_sum_y)))`. #> ℹ In group 17: `walk_number = 17`. #> Caused by warning in `log()`: #> ! NaNs produced #> ℹ Run `dplyr::last_dplyr_warnings()` to see the 4 remaining warnings. #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   prob_ruin avg_final #>       <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1      0.05      110.

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based binomial distribution (number successes n trials). Function Signature: Parameters: - .size - Number trials per step - .prob - Probability success trial Properties: - Steps integers: 0, 1, 2, …, size - Mean step = size × prob - Variance = size × prob × (1 - prob) - Symmetric prob = 0.5 Use Cases: - Quality control (defects batches) - Survey responses (yes/questions) - Medical trials (treatment successes) - Coin flip experiments Example:
code: random_binomial_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .size = 10,   .prob = 0.5,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Fair coin flips (10 per step) random_binomial_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .size = 10,   .prob = 0.5 ) |> visualize_walks() # Quality control simulation defects <- random_binomial_walk(   .num_walks = 50,   .n = 100,   .size = 100,  # Batch size   .prob = 0.05  # 5% defect rate )  defects |>   summarize_walks(.value = y, .group_var = walk_number) |>   summarize(     avg_defects_per_batch = mean(mean_val),     max_defects = max(max_val)   ) #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   avg_defects_per_batch max_defects #>                   <dbl>       <int> #> 1                  5.09          12

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based geometric distribution (number trials first success). Function Signature: Parameters: - .prob - Probability success Properties: - Steps positive integers: 1, 2, 3, … - Memoryless property - Mean = 1 / prob - Variance = (1 - prob) / prob² Use Cases: - Time first success - Reliability testing - Customer conversion time - Waiting time modeling Example:
code: random_geometric_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .prob = 0.5,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # High probability (short waits) random_geometric_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .prob = 0.8 ) |> visualize_walks() # Customer conversion modeling conversion <- random_geometric_walk(   .num_walks = 100,   .n = 50,   .prob = 0.05  # 5% conversion rate )  conversion |>   summarize_walks(.value = y) |>   pull(mean_val)  # Average trials until conversion #> [1] 19.13025

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk sampling without replacement. Function Signature: Parameters: - .m - Number white balls urn - .n - Number black balls urn - .k - Number balls drawn Properties: - Sampling without replacement - Mean = k × m / (m + n) - Used finite populations Use Cases: - Quality control sampling - Lottery probabilities - Card games - Ecological sampling Example:
code: random_hypergeometric_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .nn = 100,   .m = 50,   .n = 50,   .k = 10,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Drawing from an urn random_hypergeometric_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .m = 50,      # 50 white balls   .n = 50,  # 50 black balls   .k = 10       # Draw 10 balls ) |> visualize_walks() # Quality inspection inspection <- random_hypergeometric_walk(   .num_walks = 100,   .nn = 50,   .m = 5,        # 5 defective items   .n = 95,       # 95 good items   .k = 10        # Sample 10 items )  inspection |>   summarize_walks(.value = y) |>   pull(mean_val)  # Average defects found per sample #> [1] 0.505

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk multiple outcome categories. Function Signature: Parameters: - .size - Number trials - .prob - Vector probabilities (must sum 1) Properties: - Extension binomial multiple categories - Returns counts category - Probabilities must sum 1 Use Cases: - Survey responses multiple choices - Dice rolling - Market share analysis - Classification results Example:
code: random_multinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .size = 3,   .prob = rep(1/3, .n),   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Dice rolling (6 outcomes) random_multinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .n = 100,  # Roll 100 times   .size = 1,  # One die per roll   .prob = rep(1/6, 100)  # Fair die: 6 categories ) |> visualize_walks() # Market share simulation market_share <- random_multinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 50,   .n = 52,  # Weekly for a year   .size = 1000,  # Total customers   .prob = rep(c(0.2, 0.2, 0.35, 0.25), 13)  # Four competitors )  market_share |> visualize_walks() #> Warning: Removed 45 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range #> (`geom_line()`).

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based negative binomial (number failures r successes). Function Signature: Parameters: - .size - Target number successes - .prob - Probability success - .mu - Alternative parameterization (mean) Properties: - Overdispersed relative Poisson - Mean = size × (1 - prob) / prob - Variance = size × (1 - prob) / prob² Use Cases: - Overdispersed count data - Insurance claims - Accident modeling - Count data extra variability Example:
code: random_negbinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .size = 1,   .prob = 0.5,   .mu = NULL,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Standard negative binomial random_negbinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .size = 10,   .prob = 0.5 ) |> visualize_walks() # Overdispersed count data claims <- random_negbinomial_walk(   .num_walks = 100,   .n = 12,  # Monthly   .size = 5,   .prob = 0.3 )  claims |>   summarize_walks(.value = y, .group_var = walk_number) |>   summarize(     avg_monthly_claims = mean(mean_val),     sd_monthly_claims = mean(sd)   ) #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   avg_monthly_claims sd_monthly_claims #>                <dbl>             <dbl> #> 1               11.9              6.04

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based Poisson distribution (count events fixed interval). Function Signature: Parameters: - .lambda - Rate parameter (mean variance) Properties: - Non-negative integer steps - Mean = Variance = λ - Approximates binomial large n, small p Use Cases: - Event counts (arrivals, calls, accidents) - Rare events - Queuing theory - Web traffic - Radioactive decay Example:
code: random_poisson_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .lambda = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) # Low rate (rare events) random_poisson_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .lambda = 0.5 ) |> visualize_walks() # Call center arrivals arrivals <- random_poisson_walk(   .num_walks = 100,   .n = 24,  # Hourly for a day   .lambda = 15  # 15 calls per hour average )  arrivals |>   summarize_walks(.value = cum_sum_y, .group_var = walk_number) |>   summarize(     avg_daily_calls = mean(max_val),     max_daily_calls = max(max_val),     min_daily_calls = min(max_val)   ) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   avg_daily_calls max_daily_calls min_daily_calls #>             <dbl>           <dbl>           <dbl> #> 1            283.             327             235

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based Wilcoxon rank sum statistic. Function Signature: Parameters: - .m - Number observations first group - .k - Number observations second group Use Cases: - Nonparametric hypothesis testing - Rank-based statistics - Distribution-free methods Example:
code: random_wilcox_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .m = 10,   .k = 10,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_wilcox_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .m = 20,   .k = 10 ) |> visualize_walks()

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based Wilcoxon signed rank statistic. Function Signature: Parameters: - .nn - Number observations - .n - Integer vector. Number(s) observations sample(s) rsignrank. Default 1. Use Cases: - Paired samples testing - /comparisons - Matched pairs analysis Example:
code: random_wilcoxon_sr_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .nn = 100,   .n = 1,   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_wilcoxon_sr_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .n = 20 ) |> visualize_walks()

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Random walk based Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic distribution. Function Signature: Parameters: - .sizes - numeric vector length 2 specifying sizes parameter rsmirnov. Default c(1, 1). - .z - Optional numeric vector z parameter rsmirnov. Default NULL. - .alternative - One “two.sided” (default), “less”, “greater”. Indicates type test statistic. Use Cases: - Goodness--fit testing - Distribution comparison - Nonparametric statistics Example:
code: random_smirnov_walk(   .num_walks = 25,   .n = 100,   .sizes = c(1, 1),   .z = NULL,   .alternative = "two.sided",   .initial_value = 0,   .samp = TRUE,   .replace = TRUE,   .sample_size = 0.8,   .dimensions = 1 ) random_smirnov_walk(   .num_walks = 10,   .sizes = c(5,10) ) |> visualize_walks()

title: Discrete Distribution Generators
text: Use Poisson : - Mean ≈ Variance - Events independent - Rate constant Use Negative Binomial : - Variance > Mean (overdispersion) - Extra variability present - Poisson model doesn’t fit Use Binomial : - Fixed number trials - Binary outcomes - Independent trials

title: Double Pendulum Trajectories
text: double_pendulum_walk() models two point masses joined rigid, massless rods vertical plane. friction external forcing. Independent normal perturbations initial angles create ensemble trajectories; initialization, motion deterministic. random-waiting-time walk. Large-angle motion can chaotic, small starting differences can grow. Angles radians downward vertical, angular velocities radians per second, lengths meters, masses kilograms, time seconds. angles absolute. pivot (0, 0) positive y points upward. optional deSolve package required simulation. Install running examples unavailable. Plotting uses ggplot2; animation additionally uses gganimate, GIF rendering uses gifski.

title: Double Pendulum Trajectories
text: .n counts observations, including time zero. .n = 101 default .delta_time = 0.05, final observation five seconds. default 401 observations cover 20 seconds. Sampling intervals constrain adaptive solver’s internal integration steps. x1, y1 locate first bob; x, y locate second. positions, increments, generator add cumulative statistics. Zero angle noise produces identical trajectories identical initial states consume random numbers. Set .theta1, .theta2, .omega1, .omega2 choose starts; masses, lengths, gravity configurable.

title: Double Pendulum Trajectories
text: spatial plot shows second bob’s path, equal axis scaling color elapsed time. .walk selects walk label, position data.  visualize_walks() shows coordinate traces step number. Signed coordinates can produce undefined geometric means existing summary function; statistics changed generator.
code: plot_double_pendulum(walks, .walk = 1) summarize_walks(walks, .value = x) #> # A tibble: 1 × 17 #>   fns    fns_name dimensions   obs mean_val median range quantile_lo quantile_hi #>   <chr>  <chr>         <int> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 doubl… Double …          2   101   -0.176 -0.648  3.99       -1.98        2.00 #> # ℹ 8 more variables: variance <dbl>, sd <dbl>, min_val <dbl>, max_val <dbl>, #> #   harmonic_mean <dbl>, geometric_mean <dbl>, skewness <dbl>, kurtosis <dbl> visualize_walks(walks, .pluck = c("x", "y"))

title: Double Pendulum Trajectories
text: Construction returns customizable gganim object render save files. sampled observation becomes frame rods, bobs, pivot, elapsed time, second bob’s recent trail. Set .trail_length = 0 hide trail; otherwise counts positions including current observation. following rendering example intentionally run vignette builds: Use every sampled observation reciprocal sampling interval frame rate preserve simulated timing. Changing frame rate changes playback speed. display uses discrete states fixed spatial limits tweening.
code: animation <- animate_double_pendulum(walks, .walk = 1, .trail_length = 30) gif <- gganimate::animate(   animation,   nframes = attr(walks, "n"),   fps = 1 / attr(walks, "delta_time"),   width = 500, height = 500,   renderer = gganimate::gifski_renderer() ) gganimate::anim_save("double-pendulum.gif", animation = gif)

title: Double Pendulum Trajectories
text: implementation uses LSODA relative absolute tolerances 1e-9. equations follow double-pendulum derivation angle difference theta1 - theta2. corrects reversed difference original reference script. Long chaotic trajectories interpreted exact forecasts.

title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

what: What’s the difference between brownian_motion() and geometric_brownian_motion()?
title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
text: Brownian Motion: Can go negative, additive process Geometric Brownian Motion: Always positive, multiplicative process Use Geometric Brownian Motion modeling stock prices (can’t go negative).
code: X(t) = X(0) + μt + σW(t) X(t) = X(0) exp((μ - σ²/2)t + σW(t))

what: How do I subset walks by extremes?
title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
code: walks <- rw30()  # Get walk with maximum final value max_walk <- walks |> subset_walks(.value = "y", .type = "max")  # Get walk with minimum final value min_walk <- walks |> subset_walks(.value = "y", .type = "min")  # Visualize both walks together combined <- dplyr::bind_rows(   dplyr::mutate(max_walk, type = "Maximum"),   dplyr::mutate(min_walk, type = "Minimum") ) visualize_walks(combined, .pluck = "y") +   ggplot2::facet_wrap(~type)

what: How many walks can I generate?
title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
text: depends system, RandomWalker can handle: - Light: 1,000 walks × 1,000 steps - Moderate: 10,000 walks × 10,000 steps - Heavy: 100,000+ walks careful memory management

what: My visualization is slow. How do I speed it up?
title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
text: Reduce transparency: .alpha = 0.2 Sample walks: Show fewer walks Downsample steps: Keep every nth step Use static plots: Disable .interactive
code: # Sample walks walks_large |>   filter(walk_number %in% sample(levels(walk_number), 50)) |>   visualize_walks(.alpha = 0.2)  # Downsample steps walks_large |>   filter(step_number %% 10 == 0) |>   visualize_walks()

title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
text: functions vectorized, can use parallel processing:
code: library(future) library(furrr)  plan(multisession, workers = 4)  walks_list <- future_map(1:10, ~random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 100), .options = furrr_options(seed = 123))

code: # Generate 2D walk walk_2d <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 10, .n = 200, .dimensions = 2)  # Plot trajectories ggplot(walk_2d, aes(x = cum_sum_x, y = cum_sum_y, color = walk_number)) +   geom_path(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.5) +   geom_point(data = walk_2d %>% filter(step_number == 1),              size = 3, shape = 21, fill = "white") +  # Start points   geom_point(data = walk_2d %>% group_by(walk_number) %>% slice_max(step_number),              size = 3, shape = 24, fill = "red") +  # End points   coord_equal() +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "2D Random Walk Trajectories",     x = "X Position",     y = "Y Position",     color = "Walk"   )

code: # Generate single walk walk_2d <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 1, .n = 100, .dimensions = 2)  # Plot with step labels at intervals walk_2d_labeled <- walk_2d %>%   filter(step_number %% 10 == 0 | step_number == 1)  ggplot(walk_2d, aes(x = cum_sum_x, y = cum_sum_y)) +   geom_path(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +   geom_point(data = walk_2d_labeled, aes(color = step_number), size = 3) +   geom_text(data = walk_2d_labeled, aes(label = step_number),             hjust = -0.3, vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +   scale_color_viridis_c() +   coord_equal() +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "2D Random Walk with Step Numbers",     x = "X Position",     y = "Y Position",     color = "Step"   )

code: library(plotly) library(dplyr)  # Generate 3D walk walk_3d <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 3, .n = 100, .dimensions = 3)  # Mark start and end points walk_with_markers <- walk_3d %>%   mutate(     point_type = case_when(       step_number == 1 ~ "Start",       step_number == max(step_number) ~ "End",       TRUE ~ "Path"     )   )  # Create plot plot_ly(data = walk_with_markers) %>%   # Add paths   add_trace(     data = walk_with_markers %>% filter(point_type == "Path"),     x = ~cum_sum_x, y = ~cum_sum_y, z = ~cum_sum_z,     color = ~walk_number,     type = "scatter3d",     mode = "lines",     line = list(width = 2),     showlegend = FALSE   ) %>%   # Add start points   add_trace(     data = walk_with_markers %>% filter(point_type == "Start"),     x = ~cum_sum_x, y = ~cum_sum_y, z = ~cum_sum_z,     type = "scatter3d",     mode = "markers",     marker = list(size = 8, color = "green", symbol = "circle"),     name = "Start"   ) %>%   # Add end points   add_trace(     data = walk_with_markers %>% filter(point_type == "End"),     x = ~cum_sum_x, y = ~cum_sum_y, z = ~cum_sum_z,     type = "scatter3d",     mode = "markers",     marker = list(size = 8, color = "red", symbol = "diamond"),     name = "End"   ) %>%   layout(     title = "3D Random Walk with Start/End Markers",     scene = list(       xaxis = list(title = "X"),       yaxis = list(title = "Y"),       zaxis = list(title = "Z")     )   )

title: Statistical Analysis Guide
text: Location Measures: - mean_val: Average value across observations - median: Middle value (50th percentile) - harmonic_mean: Harmonic mean (useful rates ratios) - geometric_mean: Geometric mean (useful growth rates) Dispersion Measures: - variance: Average squared deviation mean - sd: Standard deviation (square root variance) - range: Max - Min - quantile_lo / quantile_hi: Lower upper quantiles Shape Measures: - skewness: - = 0: Symmetric distribution - > 0: Right-skewed (tail extends right) - < 0: Left-skewed (tail extends left) - kurtosis: - ≈ 3: Normal distribution - > 3: Heavy tails (extreme values) - < 3: Light tails (fewer extreme values)

text: Add cumulative calculations:
code: # Add custom cumulative functions walks_extended <- walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   mutate(     # Cumulative variance     cum_var = cumsum((y - cumsum(y) / row_number())^2) / row_number(),     # Cumulative absolute sum     cum_abs_sum = cumsum(abs(y)),     # Running maximum drawdown     running_peak = cummax(cum_sum_y),     drawdown = (cum_sum_y - running_peak) / running_peak,     max_drawdown = cummin(drawdown)   ) |>   ungroup()  # Visualize drawdown walks_extended |>   ggplot(aes(x = step_number, y = max_drawdown, color = walk_number)) +   geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(title = "Maximum Drawdown Over Time")

code: # 3D walk walks_3d <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 1000, .dimensions = 3)  # Calculate distance walks_with_dist <- walks_3d |> euclidean_distance(.x = x, .y = z)  # Analyze distance evolution distance_stats <- walks_with_dist |>   group_by(step_number) |>   summarize(     mean_dist = mean(distance),     sd_dist = sd(distance),     max_dist = max(distance)   )  # Plot average distance vs sqrt(n) theoretical prediction distance_stats |>   ggplot(aes(x = step_number)) +   geom_line(aes(y = mean_dist, color = "Observed"), linewidth = 1) +   geom_line(aes(y = sqrt(3 * step_number), color = "Theory"), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "blue", "Theory" = "red")) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Mean Distance vs Theoretical Prediction",     subtitle = "Distance ~ sqrt(3n) for 3D Brownian motion",     x = "Step",     y = "Distance",     color = ""   ) #> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range #> (`geom_line()`).

text: Calculate walks first reach threshold:
code: # Generate walks walks <- discrete_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 1000, .initial_value = 0)  # Find first passage time to level 10 first_passage <- walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   filter(cum_sum_y >= 10) |>   slice_min(step_number, n = 1) |>   select(walk_number, first_passage_time = step_number)  # Analyze distribution of first passage times first_passage |>   ggplot(aes(x = first_passage_time)) +   geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(     title = "Distribution of First Passage Times to Level 10",     x = "First Passage Time (Steps)",     y = "Count"   )

text: Extract walks extreme values:
code: # Generate walks walks <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 100, .initial_value = 100)  # Get walk with maximum final value max_walk <- walks |> subset_walks(.value = "cum_sum_y", .type = "max")  # Get walk with minimum final value min_walk <- walks |> subset_walks(.value = "cum_sum_y", .type = "min")  # Show the extreme walks max_walk |>    summarize_walks(.value = cum_sum_y, .group_var = walk_number) #> # A tibble: 1 × 18 #>   walk_number fns    fns_name dimensions   obs mean_val median range quantile_lo #>   <fct>       <chr>  <chr>         <dbl> <int>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 21          rando… Random …          1   100     101.   101.  2.86        100. #> # ℹ 9 more variables: quantile_hi <dbl>, variance <dbl>, sd <dbl>, #> #   min_val <dbl>, max_val <dbl>, harmonic_mean <dbl>, geometric_mean <dbl>, #> #   skewness <dbl>, kurtosis <dbl>  min_walk |>    summarize_walks(.value = cum_sum_y, .group_var = walk_number) #> # A tibble: 1 × 18 #>   walk_number fns    fns_name dimensions   obs mean_val median range quantile_lo #>   <fct>       <chr>  <chr>         <dbl> <int>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 66          rando… Random …          1   100     98.3   98.3  2.84        97.2 #> # ℹ 9 more variables: quantile_hi <dbl>, variance <dbl>, sd <dbl>, #> #   min_val <dbl>, max_val <dbl>, harmonic_mean <dbl>, geometric_mean <dbl>, #> #   skewness <dbl>, kurtosis <dbl>

title: Statistical Analysis Guide
code: # Generate walks walks <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 100)  # Test if steps are normally distributed steps <- walks |> pull(y)  # Shapiro-Wilk test for normality shapiro.test(sample(steps, 5000))  # Sample for computational efficiency #>  #>  Shapiro-Wilk normality test #>  #> data:  sample(steps, 5000) #> W = 0.99943, p-value = 0.1313  # Q-Q plot qqnorm(steps) qqline(steps)

title: Statistical Analysis Guide
text: Test random walk hypothesis:
code: # Generate walk walk <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 1, .n = 1000)  # Calculate variance ratio values <- walk |> pull(cum_sum_y)  # Variance of k-differences k <- 10 var_k <- var(diff(values, lag = k)) var_1 <- var(diff(values, lag = 1))  # Variance ratio (should be ≈ k for random walk) vr <- var_k / (k * var_1) print(paste("Variance Ratio:", round(vr, 3), "| Expected:", k)) #> [1] "Variance Ratio: 1.014 | Expected: 10"

title: Statistical Analysis Guide
code: # Generate stock price simulation prices <- geometric_brownian_motion(   .num_walks = 1,   .n = 252,   .mu = 0.08,   .sigma = 0.25,   .initial_value = 100 )  # Calculate returns returns <- prices |>   mutate(     log_return = log(cum_prod_y / lag(cum_prod_y)),     simple_return = (cum_prod_y - lag(cum_prod_y)) / lag(cum_prod_y)   ) |>   filter(!is.na(log_return))  # Analyze returns returns |>   summarize(     mean_return = mean(log_return) * 252,  # Annualized     volatility = sd(log_return) * sqrt(252),  # Annualized     sharpe_ratio = mean_return / volatility   ) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   mean_return volatility sharpe_ratio #>         <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl> #> 1        144.      0.928         155.

title: Statistical Analysis Guide
code: # Generate two types of walks normal_walks <- random_normal_walk(.num_walks = 50, .n = 100) cauchy_walks <- random_cauchy_walk(.num_walks = 50, .n = 100)  # Get final values normal_final <- normal_walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   slice_max(step_number) |>   pull(cum_sum_y)  cauchy_final <- cauchy_walks |>   group_by(walk_number) |>   slice_max(step_number) |>   pull(cum_sum_y)  # Wilcoxon rank-sum test (non-parametric) wilcox.test(normal_final, cauchy_final) #>  #>  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction #>  #> data:  normal_final and cauchy_final #> W = 1266, p-value = 0.9149 #> alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 # Kolmogorov-Smirnov test ks.test(normal_final, cauchy_final) #>  #>  Exact two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test #>  #> data:  normal_final and cauchy_final #> D = 0.48, p-value = 1.387e-05 #> alternative hypothesis: two-sided

code: # Generate walk with known drift walks <- random_normal_drift_walk(.num_walks = 100, .n = 100, .mu = 0.1)  # Test if mean step is significantly different from 0 steps <- walks |> pull(y) t.test(steps, mu = 0) #>  #>  One Sample t-test #>  #> data:  steps #> t = 115.67, df = 9999, p-value < 2.2e-16 #> alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0 #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  10.10977 10.45834 #> sample estimates: #> mean of x  #>  10.28405
